extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and judges (English/common-law patent practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for construing letters patent and for the property, assignment, and enforcement of patent rights under English law; includes procedural requirements (enrolment), limits on assignment, effects of invalidity, bankruptcy issues, and parliamentary interventions. Geared to legal/practical handling of patents and related disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule of construction between subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Between subject and subject, the principle of construction is that the grant shall be construed, if the meaning be doubtful, most strongly against the grantor, who is presumed to use the most cautious words for his own advantage and security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting ordinary (non-royal) grants, ambiguous terms should be read against the grantor; use ordinary-rules of contra proferentem for private grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of royal grants (Crown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal grants have at all times been construed most favourably for the King where a fair doubt exists as to the real meaning of the instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This favourable construction for the Crown is subject to many limitations: no strained or extravagant construction in favour of the King; if the intention is obvious, give a fair and liberal interpretation accordingly; a recital will not restrain an expressed granting part if the granting part plainly expresses the Crown's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions leaning in favour of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction shall lean in favour of the subject if the grant shows it was not made at the solicitation of the grantee (ex speciali gratia, certi scienti, et mero motu regis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a grant appears to have been granted as a special favour rather than at the grantee's solicitation, interpretation principles that favor the subject may apply despite it being a Crown grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of valuable consideration on construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the King's grant is upon a valuable consideration, it shall be construed strictly for the patentee for the honour of the King.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a valuable consideration has been given, prefer a construction that preserves and gives effect to the grant (choose the interpretation that validates the grant if two constructions exist, one making it void).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty requirement for grants
rubrics_metrics.description: A decided uncertainty will avoid a grant from the Crown (and generally); the rule 'certum est quod certum reddi potest' applies — a grant must be capable of being rendered certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject-matter is indeterminate such that it cannot be made certain, the grant may be void. Where a particular certainty precedes, it will not be destroyed by later mistake or uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrecitals and deceit invalidate grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrecitals and false suggestions or deceit will in certain cases invalidate a grant from the Crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of deceit or materially false recitals can negate the grant; courts may treat such grants as void where fraud is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents for inventions construed for the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: The exposition of patents for inventions is a statement of the statute of monopolies, to be explained most liberally to the subject's (patentee's) advantage; patents contain expressions (ex speciali gratia, certi scienti, et mero motu) and a clause that patents shall be construed in the most favourable and beneficial sense for the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing patent grants and specifications, courts will generally favor the patentee, especially where the patentee has made a fair disclosure; nevertheless this favorable approach is balanced against preventing imposition on the public when disclosure is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and specification must be read together
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent and specification must be taken together when considering the proper construction of the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of the patent text cannot ignore the specification; the disclosure in the specification is integral to what the patent covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (specification requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it appears that the patentee has made a fair disclosure, the patentee is entitled to the protection the law gives him; conversely where the discovery is not fully made, the court must look with a very watchful eye to prevent imposition on the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that enables a machinist to make the machine (i.e., communicates the invention to the public) satisfies the statute. Insufficient disclosure may defeat the patent or limit its scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents must stand or fall by their own terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent and specification must, in fact, stand or fall by themselves; no extraneous matter can be introduced to explain them and establish their legality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not use external legislative acts or extrinsic evidence to validate an otherwise invalid patent instrument; the intrinsic text governs validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: The privilege is allowed to be enjoyed for fourteen years or under; the term is to be accounted from the date of the first letters patent or grant; a patent attempting to extend beyond fourteen years would be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents exceeding statutory maximum duration are invalid; check grant date and any statutory extensions separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of persons interested (assignment cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the person interested in the patent should make any transfer or assignment, divide it into shares, declare a trust, seek public subscriptions, or do anything so that more than five persons should in any manner become interested and claim a benefit in the patent, it is declared to be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent cannot be assigned or held so that more than five persons are beneficially interested (unless Parliament intervenes to enlarge that number). Executors and administrators count as the single person they represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of patent as personal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to restrictions as to duration and number of persons, a patent may be assigned in the same manner as other personal property; the property in a patent is a personal chattel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments follow ordinary personal property rules; ensure assignments respect statutory caps and formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patent invalidity on enforcement and covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee brings an action for breach of covenant/for infringement, it may be answered by showing in any manner that the patent is a bad one and invalid; where a patentee seeks to re-assert rights contrary to his own assignment, equity may prevent him from denying conveyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants can raise invalidity as a defence to enforcement; but where assignor breaches covenant and then denies the conveyance, courts may prevent inequitable conduct. Consider estoppel and equitable limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and purchaser's loss when patent proves invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee who has used the patent and paid for it cannot recover the purchase-money if the grant later proves bad; if invalidity is discovered before any use, equitable principles suggest the purchase-money may be returned, provided no fraud is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where both parties innocently contracted under a mistaken belief in validity, the loss may be borne differently depending on use and fraud; no recovery if assignee has used the invention and derived benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licences and licensee rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee may grant licences to persons to use his patent; in the event of infringement it would appear that all who have licences may maintain actions for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees (properly authorized) can sue for infringement/damages; licensors should document licence terms plainly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary enlargement and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament may extend a patent's term or increase the number of persons who may be interested; such acts typically include a proviso that every objection in law competent against the patent shall be of the same force against the act; but an act of Parliament does not by itself change the intrinsic validity of the patent—patent and specification still must stand by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of Parliament granting extensions or assignment rights usually do not cure intrinsic defects in the patent; check for provisos preserving legal objections and do not rely on parliamentary recital to validate a defective patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusts in relation to patents
rubrics_metrics.description: It was doubted whether letters patent generally could be subject of a trust, but a patent for an invention might become so in the same manner as other personal property; expressly allowed that it shall not be assigned in trust to more than five persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents can be placed in trust subject to the five-person cap; structure trusts to comply with statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy effects on patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent will pass to the assignees of a bankrupt patentee; a grant obtained by an uncertificated bankrupt since the act of bankruptcy is affected by the previous assignment of the commissioners and is liable to seizure by assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees facing bankruptcy should seek renunciations from assignees if intending to exploit schemes before certificate; creditors' assignees may assert rights in patents obtained after bankruptcy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrolment of improved specification (procedural requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject of the patent has been gradually improved, the act provides that a specification of the whole invention, in its improved state, shall be enrolled in the Court of Chancery within a given time, which is generally six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely enrolment of an improved specification (typically within six months) is required to reflect improvements; failure to enrol may affect validity or enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No exclusive property in unpatented secret discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who keep their discoveries secret and use or vend their manufacture without the protection of a patent do not have an exclusive right in such a subject; there is not any rule of law preventing others from making use of such manufactures unless fraud is practised in obtaining the secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secrecy alone does not create a legal monopoly — remedies arise only if fraud or other actionable wrong occurs in acquiring the secret. Inventors must weigh secrecy against patent protection.
